title: The divisor lattice is a product of chains with a symmetric rank polynomial

status: Classical result or newly stipulated finite model; historical claims explicitly delimited
summary: The source gives D(360) as C₄×C₃×C₂ and links rank coefficients to τ and lattice height to Ω. These statements admit a direct complete proof, with a useful rank symmetry that goes beyond merely counting divisors.
definitions_json: ["If n=∏p_i^{a_i}, order its positive divisors by divisibility. Represent d=∏p_i^{b_i} by the vector (b_i), 0≤b_i≤a_i. Give it rank ρ(d)=Σb_i.","Let R_n(t)=Σ_{d|n}t^{ρ(d)} and Ω(n)=Σa_i. A chain C_{a_i+1} is the totally ordered set {0,…,a_i}."]

theorem_statement: D(n)≅∏C_{a_i+1} as lattices, with meet and join given by coordinate minima and maxima. R_n(t)=∏(1+t+⋯+t^{a_i}); R_n(1)=τ(n), its degree is Ω(n), and t^{Ω(n)}R_n(t^{−1})=R_n(t).

Divisibility is coordinatewise inequality, so greatest lower and least upper bounds are coordinatewise minimum and maximum, proving the lattice isomorphism. Multiplying the finite geometric polynomials records every independent choice of b_i once, proving the rank formula. Substitution t=1 counts all choices and hence all divisors. The top vector has rank Σa_i, and every saturated chain from bottom to top increments one exponent at a time, giving that height in edges. The involution d↦n/d replaces each b_i by a_i−b_i and reverses rank, proving coefficient symmetry and the reciprocal polynomial identity. Thus not only τ and Ω, but the full rank distribution, is determined by the species.

Complementary ranks zero/six, one/five and two/four have matching counts. title: Two-sector failure has a correlation parameter and a rigorous confidence envelope

title: Base twelve changes representation while preserving exact arithmetic
revised_question: Which rational numbers have finite duodecimal expansions, and how are periodic expansions certified?
status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
summary: The July31 language discussion includes base twelve and symbolic representation. Its mathematical core is a division algorithm, not a change in the underlying rational numbers. Exact remainder orbits give terminating and repeating expansions with unambiguous conventions.
definitions_json: ["Use digits0,…,9,A,B for values0,…,11. For a rational0≤a/b<1 in lowest terms, long division sets r₀=a,12r_j=b d_{j+1}+r_{j+1}, with0≤r_{j+1}<b. A bar denotes infinite repetition."]

theorem_statement: The base-twelve expansion of a/b terminates exactly when b divides12^N for some N, equivalently b has no prime factors except2 and3. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion; after removing the2- and3-parts of the denominator, the period divides the multiplicative order of12 modulo its remaining part.
theorem_proof: AfterN steps the division identities telescope to a/b=Σ_{j=1}^N d_j12^{-j}+r_N/(b12^N). Termination is equivalent to r_N=0 and hence to b|12^N because gcd(a,b)=1. Conversely that divisibility forces zero remainder. Only finitely many remainders occur, so a nonzero remainder must eventually repeat and the deterministic update then repeats forever. When the denominator is coprime to12, the remainder is12^j a modb and the first return occurs at the multiplicative order of12. Powers of2 and3 contribute only a finite preperiod. An expansion ending in infinitely manyB digits is the familiar alternate representation of a terminating number; choosing the non-B-tail convention restores uniqueness. The same remainder identity certifies truncation error without a decimal approximation: afterN digits the omitted fraction is exactlyr_N/(b12^N), betweenzero and12^{-N}. For a repeating block oflengthh, multiplying by12^h and subtracting yields a rational denominator12^h−1. These two identities provide exact conversion in both directions.

For1/5 the remainders follow1→2→4→3→1 and the digits are2,4,9,7. Thus1/5=.overline{2497}₁₂; equivalently(2·12³+4·12²+9·12+7)/(12⁴−1)=4147/20735=1/5.","conclusion":"Each symbolic statement reduces to an integer identity and a finite remainder certificate."}

summary: The July31 source proposes square-free reduction, Pellet/Graeffe filters and a universal polynomial-solving atlas. A useful classical atlas certifies where roots are and how many occur. It does not bypass the obstruction to general radical formulas.

On|z|=3,27>12+1 proves all three inside; hence exactly two lie in1<|z|<3. Forq, E(y)=y+2 and O(y)=−3, soG(y)=(y+2)²−9y=y²−5y+4, with roots1 and4, the squares of1 and2.","conclusion":"The output is a finite exact counting certificate with stated disks and multiplicities."}

title: A contraction certificate gives a genuinely guaranteed Newton enclosure
revised_question: What finite inequalities prove existence and uniqueness of a root in a chosen interval?
status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
summary: The late-July universal-solving discussion is made constructive by replacing an unqualified convergence promise with a local certificate. A fixed inverse-Jacobian approximation produces a contraction whose hypotheses can be checked with rational bounds.
definitions_json: ["Let f be continuously differentiable on I=[c−r,c+r], choose a nonzero constant C, and set T(x)=x−Cf(x). Assume sup_I|1−Cf′(x)|≤q<1."]

Completeness and the contraction theorem give a unique fixed point. SinceC≠0, fixed points are exactly zeros off. The same argument bounds the distance from an iterate to the root by|T(x)−x|/(1−q). Every hypothesis is local and explicit. A convergence plot or small residual is weaker: for example a nearly singular derivative can make a tiny residual coexist with a substantial root error. In several variables the analogous test uses a norm bound forI−CJF throughout a box and an inclusion test for its centered image. A practical certificate may choose a fixedC rather than recomputingf′(x)^{-1} at each step. This makes the map and its derivative bound uniform on the entire interval. The inclusion bound is1/70+1/3500=51/3500<1/50=70/3500. Thus there is exactly one root in[1.38,1.42], and the fixed-inverse iteration converges from every point of this interval. status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
summary: The July31 representation discussion includes rationals, reals and p-adics. A valuation makes this distinction precise: it changes which approximations are small, while preserving ordinary algebraic equalities on the embedded rational field. Root lifting provides a constructive rather than purely metaphorical example.

Since|p^N|_p=p^{-N}→0, completeness gives the stated limit; the real terms instead grow and their partial sums diverge. For lifting supposef(r_n)≡0 modp^n andtryr_{n+1}=r_n+t p^n with0≤t<p. title: A cutoff theorem with the quantifiers made explicit
revised_question: When does increasing approximation resolution remain compatible with vanishing data noise, uniformly over a specified model class?
status: Proved under the stated hypotheses; newly stipulated examples
summary: The recovered master inequality becomes useful only after the model class, data norm and quantifiers are fixed. The fundamental issue is that approximation can improve while noise amplification becomes arbitrarily large. A diagonal parameter choice reconciles these two limits without requiring a guessed convergence rate.
definitions_json: ["Let A:X→Y be bounded between normed spaces, let M⊂X be a specified nonempty class, and let R_n:Y→X be bounded linear maps. Data satisfy yδ=Ax+e with ||e||≤δ.","Define B_M(n)=sup_{x∈M}||R_nAx−x||, S(n)=||R_n||, and Eδ(R_n;M)=sup_{x∈M,||e||≤δ}||R_n(Ax+e)−x||. Assume B_M(n) is finite and tends to zero."]
theorem_name: Uniform bias–noise decomposition and diagonal regularization
theorem_statement: Eδ(R_n;M)≤B_M(n)+δS(n). There exists an integer choice n(δ)→∞ with Eδ(R_{n(δ)};M)→0. Every choice with B_M(n(δ))→0 and δS(n(δ))→0 has this property.
theorem_proof: Add and subtract R_nAx and apply the triangle inequality and the operator norm bound. For existence choose a strictly increasing sequence n_j with B_M(n_j)≤1/j. Put s_j=max(1,S(n_1),…,S(n_j)), and choose strictly decreasing positive d_j→0 with d_j≤1/(j s_j). For d_{j+1}<δ≤d_j use n(δ)=n_j. Then δS(n(δ))≤1/j and the total bound is at most 2/j. As δ→0 the interval index j→∞, hence the result. This proof does not assume that S is monotone or that B has a power-law rate. Uniform convergence of B is a substantive hypothesis: pointwise convergence R_nAx→x for each fixed x does not imply it on an arbitrary unbounded class. If A has a nonzero kernel and M contains x and x+h with h∈ker A, a uniform error tending to zero is impossible, since the data coincide. Thus the model class must encode identifiable information as well as approximation smoothness.

title: Mild ill-posedness: an optimal rate from a concrete ellipsoid
revised_question: Can the polynomial cutoff rate be proved with both an upper bound and a matching impossibility argument?
status: Proved under the stated hypotheses; newly stipulated examples
summary: The source rate δ^{r/(p+r)} has a clean deterministic interpretation. It is the minimax order for a diagonal operator with polynomial singular values and a Sobolev-type ellipsoid. A two-point indistinguishability argument supplies the lower bound, so the rate expresses an information limitation rather than only the quality of one algorithm.
definitions_json: ["Take X=Y=ℓ², Ae_k=k^(−p)e_k with p>0, and M_r={x:Σk^{2r}|x_k|²≤1}, r>0. Let R_N invert the first N coordinates and discard the rest.","The deterministic minimax error is inf over all maps T:Y→X of sup_{x∈M_r,||e||≤δ}||T(Ax+e)−x||. The map T need not be linear or continuous."]

theorem_statement: For sufficiently small δ>0, spectral cutoff with N=⌊δ^(−1/(p+r))⌋ has worst-case error O(δ^{r/(p+r)}). No reconstruction map improves this order uniformly on M_r under norm-bounded noise.

The stated N balances the two terms and gives the upper order. For the lower bound put K=⌈δ^(−1/(p+r))⌉ and v=K^(−r)e_K. Both v and −v belong to M_r and ||Av||=K^(−(p+r))≤δ. The observation zero can thus arise from v with noise −Av or from −v with noise Av. For any output z=T(0), the triangle inequality gives max(||z−v||,||z+v||)≥||v||. Since K≤2δ^(−1/(p+r)) for δ≤1, this is at least 2^(−r)δ^{r/(p+r)}. This applies to every possible estimator. It also explains why stronger algorithms alone cannot remove the smoothness–noise tradeoff.

title: Tikhonov filters: qualification and explicit constants
revised_question: How do a spectral source condition and the filter maximum produce a complete Tikhonov error estimate?
status: Proved under the stated hypotheses; newly stipulated examples
summary: The filter formula in the recovered manuscript can be strengthened into an explicit theorem, including the range of smoothness for which the simple argument works. The parameter α controls both spectral bias and amplification; the source exponent determines their balance.
definitions_json: ["Let A:X→Y be bounded between Hilbert spaces and define R_α=(A* A+αI)^(−1)A*, α>0. Assume x†=(A* A)^νw, ||w||≤ρ, with 0<ν≤1.","The source condition places x† in ker(A) perpendicular and specifies spectral smoothness. Fractional powers are defined by the spectral calculus of the nonnegative bounded self-adjoint operator A* A."]

Differentiating log(t^ν/(1+t)) gives ν/t−1/(1+t), so the maximum occurs at t=ν/(1−ν) when0<ν<1 and equals cν. Atν=1 the supremum is1. The noise multiplier is √λ/(λ+α); its derivative vanishes at λ=α and its global maximum is1/(2√α). The spectral theorem and the triangle inequality give the bound. Balancing α^νρ with δα^(−1/2) gives the parameter order and rate. title: Landweber iteration: regularization by stopping
revised_question: How can an iterative algorithm converge for exact data yet need early stopping for noisy data?
status: Proved under the stated hypotheses; newly stipulated examples
summary: The recovered Landweber filter makes the role of iteration count precise. Increasing m shrinks the spectral residual and increases the noise norm. The same controlled-approximation principle used for spectral cutoff therefore governs an algorithm with no explicit truncation.

title: The ignition constant: a proved integral behind an unverified front law
revised_question: What can be established exactly about C0 without recovering the original front ODE or treating numerical agreement as its proof?
status: Proved under the stated hypotheses; newly stipulated examples
summary: The recovered integral is a well-defined mathematical object even though the governing front equation and normalization did not survive retrieval. It admits strict bounds, a positive rational series and controlled numerical quadrature. These results support a conditional interpretation of the reported large-Z law without inventing its missing derivation.
definitions_json: ["Put s(t)=(1+t)e^(−t) for t≥0, h(t)=1−√(1−s(t)), and C0=∫_0^∞h(t)dt. Then0<s(t)≤1, s is strictly decreasing for t>0, and h is decreasing from1 to0.","Let a_k=binom(2k,k)/(4^k(2k−1)) for k≥1, so1−√(1−z)=Σ_{k≥1}a_kz^k for0≤z≤1. Every coefficient is positive andΣa_k=1."]
theorem_name: Exact bounds and a monotone rational series
theorem_statement: 1<C0<2 and C0=Σ_{k≥1}a_k Σ_{j=0}^k binom(k,j)j!/k^{j+1}. If S_K is the sum through K, then S_K<C0<S_K+2(1−Σ_{k≤K}a_k). All finite quantities in this enclosure are rational.
theorem_proof: Rationalize h=s/(1+√(1−s)). Since the denominator lies strictly between1 and2 for t>0, s/2<h<s there. The integral of s is2, proving the strict bounds and convergence. The binomial series has nonnegative terms, so monotone convergence permits integrating it term by term, including near t=0 where s=1. Expand(1+t)^k and use∫_0^∞t^j e^(−kt)dt=j!/k^{j+1}. This proves the series. For the tail, s(t)^k≤s(t) for everyk≥1; hence∫s^k≤2. Sum the omitted coefficients to obtain the rational upper error bound. The resulting enclosure is deliberately elementary rather than an efficient high-precision algorithm. For numerical work, monotonicity bounds the finite integral by left and right rectangles, whose difference is at most the step width. The tail after L is at most∫_L^∞s=(L+2)e^(−L). A floating implementation of those bounds still needs exponential rounding control before it becomes an interval-arithmetic certificate.

title: A singular descriptor matrix can encode a regular constrained system
revised_question: When is singular E legitimate, and what goes wrong if it is repaired by adding εI?
status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
summary: The August2 source correctly distinguishes differential–algebraic structure from malformed data. Singular E does not imply a singular matrix pencil. A two-dimensional exact example shows how regularization can create a large unstable eigenvalue absent from the original constrained dynamics.

theorem_name: Constraint preservation versus a spurious fast mode
theorem_statement: For E=diag(1,0), A=diag(−1,1), the pencil is regular, the only finite eigenvalue is−1, and consistent trajectories have x₂=0. Replacing E by E+εI, ε>0, introduces an unstable eigenvalue1/ε.
theorem_proof: The original equations are ẋ₁=−x₁ and0=x₂. Thus all consistent solutions are x(t)=(ae^{−t},0). The determinant det(A−λE)=−1−λ is not the zero polynomial; its degree one in a two-dimensional pencil accounts for one infinite eigenvalue. The algebraic component is a constraint, not a hidden differential state that may be evolved arbitrarily. After regularization, the equations become(1+ε)ẋ₁=−x₁ andεẋ₂=x₂, with eigenvalues−1/(1+ε) and1/ε. Any nonzero error in the constrained coordinate grows as e^{t/ε}. A pseudoinverse replacement also changes the equations unless its constraint consistency is separately enforced. Descriptor-native reduction instead retains the finite deflating subspace and algebraic constraints; an index or minimal-index assertion additionally requires the appropriate canonical data.

theorem_statement: T_i∈SU(5), they satisfy the braid relation, and (T₁T₂)³=I. If additionally T_i³⁴=I, they define a quotient of Δ(2,3,34). Moreover G≅SU(5)×μ₁₇ as compact groups, via (S,ξ)↦ξS.
theorem_proof: Twisting a5×5 matrix by ζ⁵ multiplies its determinant by ζ²⁵; thus det T_i=ζ³⁴=1. Both sides of the braid relation gain the same scalar ζ¹⁵. The central relation gains ζ³⁰, cancelling ζ⁴ because ζ³⁴=1. Put a=T₁T₂T₁ and b=T₁T₂. The braid relation gives a²=b³=I, and b⁻¹a=T₁, so the extra relation T₁³⁴=I gives the triangle presentation with orders dividing2,3,34. For the group decomposition, ξ∈μ₁₇ has determinant ξ⁵. Since5 is invertible modulo17, this scalar determinant map is an automorphism; its inverse exponent is7. Given g∈G, set ξ=det(g)⁷ and S=ξ⁻¹g. Then det S=det(g)^(1−35)=1. This is a continuous inverse to (S,ξ)↦ξS, and the intersection SU(5)∩μ₁₇I is trivial, proving the product isomorphism.

title: Shared uncertainty should be optimized jointly in a decision difference
revised_question: How can a decision be certified when separate interval bounds overlap but the competing scores share the same uncertainty?
status: Classical mathematics or a newly chosen finite model developed with proof; historical claims delimited
summary: The recovered final October target is to certify a decision using common uncertainty and the cheapest sufficient measurement. Joint modeling preserves cancellation that is destroyed by independent interval bounds. The following theorem is deterministic and concerns abstract scores, with no empirical or financial forecast assumed.
definitions_json: ["Let X be a nonempty uncertainty set and let J_A,J_B:X→R be two scores, with larger preferred. Set δ(x)=J_A(x)−J_B(x).","A strict robust certificate is a positive lower bound m≤inf_(x∈X)δ(x). Attainment of the infimum is unnecessary if a bound is proved directly."]
theorem_name: Joint dominance and measurement certificates
theorem_statement: If inf_X(J_A−J_B)>0, A wins for every compatible state. In the shared model J_A=c+δ, J_B=c with δ∈[7/4,9/4], the margin is at least 7/4 regardless of the range of c. Separate interval subtraction can fail to certify the same fact.
theorem_proof: The first assertion is immediate from the defining inequality for every x. Its content is the order of operations: subtraction must take place at the same uncertainty state before minimization. In general inf(A−B)≥inf A−sup B, but the inequality can be strict because the separate extrema need not occur at compatible states. For c∈[0,100], separate score ranges are A∈[7/4,409/4] and B∈[0,100]; their interval difference includes −393/4, even though the exact shared difference is always positive. A new measurement with result z and error bound ε restricts X to X_z={x:|h(x)−z|≤ε}; computing the margin on X_z can only improve its lower bound because X_z⊆X. A decision-sufficient experiment is one whose every nonempty outcome fibre gives a positive margin for one of the two directions.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Suppose δ itself is measured with absolute error at most 1/10.","calculation":"A result z=1/4 implies δ≥z−1/10=3/20>0, certifying A. A result z=1/20 gives δ∈[−1/20,3/20], so it does not certify either direction. With several possible tests, their costs and outcome fibres can be inserted into the finite Bellman recurrence to identify the cheapest guaranteed decision procedure.","conclusion":"The certificate exploits correlation exactly and states which remaining uncertainty matters."}
limits: Overlapping separate intervals do not imply an undecidable joint model, while a positive estimate without an error bound is not a robust certificate. This theorem supplies no calibration of an empirical uncertainty set.
extension: Use polynomial or rational score models on a semialgebraic X and produce an exact positivity certificate for J_A−J_B; then optimize measurement cost subject to such certificates on every admissible outcome fibre.

title: Five raw observations determine the entire 107-bit generator state
revised_question: Can the reported raw-state uniqueness be proved for every state with a small, independently checkable exact certificate?
status: New exact all-state certificate, independently replayable with standard-library Python
summary: The explicit recurrence allows a global theorem stronger than a collection of decoding tests. Equality of output words becomes a short-vector problem in an integer lattice. Exact dual bounds exclude every nonzero collision at once. The supplied certificate covers all 126  choices of five positions within nine steps; no enumeration of2^107 states and no trust in an LLL implementation is required.
definitions_json: ["Let M=2^107−1, A=3^121 moduloM, and b=2^26. States are integers0≤x_i<M with x_{i+1}=Ax_i moduloM; the raw observation is y_i=x_i modulo b. Since M≡1 modulo3, A is invertible moduloM.","For positions0≤p_0<⋯<p_4≤8 put g_j=p_j−p_0 and Λ_p={d∈Z^5:d_j≡A^{g_j}d_0 moduloM forj=1,…,4}. Let D=⌊(M−1)/b⌋=2^81−1."]
theorem_name: Exact raw-state observability
theorem_statement: For every five-position subset of{0,…,8}, the selected raw words uniquely determine the initial state. Four raw words cannot determine every state. Every supplied integer basis B_p has rows inΛ_p, |det B_p|=M^4, and DΣ_i|(B_p^(−1))_{ij}|<3/8 for each columnj.
theorem_proof:
The homomorphism Z^5→(Z/MZ)^4 sending d to(d_j−A^{g_j}d_0)_{j=1}^4 is onto: vary the final four coordinates while keeping d_0=0. Its kernelΛ_p therefore has indexM^4. The checker verifies lattice membership of every basis row and determinant magnitudeM^4, proving that its row lattice equalsΛ_p rather than merely a sublattice. It computes the inverse over rational numbers, verifies B_pB_p^(−1)=I, and checks the strict column bounds for all 126 position subsets. These properties alone suffice; the LLL routine used to find the bases is not trusted.

Suppose two states have the same five observed words. At each selected step their state difference is b d_j for an integerd_j with |d_j|≤D. The recurrence implies d_j≡A^{g_j}d_0 moduloM because b is invertible moduloM. Hence d=cB_p for some integer rowc. Each coordinate satisfies |c_j|=|(dB_p^(−1))_j|≤DΣ_i|(B_p^(−1))_{ij}|<3/8<1. Thusc=0, all selected state differences vanish, and invertibility of A takes equality atp_0 back to equality of the initial states. Four words range over at mostb^4=2^104 possibilities, whereas even the nonzero state set has M−1>2^104 elements. Pigeonhole therefore proves four-word impossibility.

The same dual bounds yield a decoder. Write selected states as y_j+bz_j with0≤z_j≤D. Their congruences define an affine lattice v+Λ_p, using v_0=0 and v_j=b^(−1)(A^{g_j}y_0−y_j) moduloM. For z=v+cB_p, each integerc_j lies in the exact interval obtained by applying the corresponding inverse column to the box0≤z≤D. Its width is below3/8, so it contains at most one integer. Round the interval endpoints exactly, reconstruct z and check all state bounds and observations; then reverse A^{p_0}. This is an actual exact decoder, not only an existence result.

Its decoder recovers all 630 specified state/pattern fixtures, including boundary states. The largest dual bound is checked as an exact rational number strictly below3/8; its floating display, about0.368314147, is only for reading.","conclusion":"The universal conclusion comes from the determinant and dual-bound proof. limits: Raw observations are consecutive generator steps at known positions, with the source recurrence and output convention stated above. Rejected/accepted-output sequences have hidden step counts and require a different theorem. This certificate makes no claim about their six-output threshold.
extension: Certify additional sparse position patterns, derive the smallest alphabet width permitting five-observation recovery, and optimize the rational basis for a low-cost decoder while retaining exactly the same independent determinant/dual-bound checks.

title: Seven and nine raw observations have optimal one- and two-error correction
revised_question: What error correction follows from the all-state observation theorem, and are the observation counts information-theoretically necessary?
status: New exact all-state certificate, independently replayable with standard-library Python
summary: The finite-state trajectories define a code over the alphabet of26-bit words. The five-observation theorem controls its minimum Hamming distance without requiring linearity over a field. A puncturing argument then proves that the seven- and nine-word correction lengths cannot be improved for this full state population.
definitions_json: ["For5≤n≤9 let C_n={c_n(x):0≤x<M}, where c_n(x)=(y_0,…,y_{n−1}) is the raw trajectory. Hamming distance counts differing words, regardless of the bit distance within a corrupted word.","An arbitrary word corruption replaces one entire26-bit symbol. Unique correction oftcorruptions requires minimum code distance at least2t+1. Erasures at known positions are a different, easier observation model."]
theorem_name: Exact distance and length-optimal correction
theorem_statement: For5≤n≤9 the minimum distance of C_n is exactlyn−4. Thus seven raw outputs correct one arbitrary word error, and nine correct two. No code representing all M states over this alphabet can correct one error with six words or two errors with eight words.
theorem_proof:
If two distinct state codewords agreed at five positions in any n≤9, the preceding theorem would make the states equal. They therefore agree in at most four positions, giving distance at leastn−4. Conversely, for any code of minimum distanced, puncturing d−1fixed positions leaves an injective map: otherwise two original words differed only in those positions, contradicting the distance. Hence its population is at mostb^{n−d+1}. Since M>b^4, one has n−d+1≥5, or d≤n−4. This proves equality.

Two Hamming balls of radius t are disjoint when the minimum distance exceeds2t, by the triangle inequality; hence the stated seven- and nine-word codes uniquely correct the stated errors. An explicit decoder enumerates five-position subsets, applies the certified affine-lattice decoder, re-encodes each candidate and retains a state within the permitted Hamming radius. Enough clean positions remain to produce the true candidate, and the distance proof rules out a second one. Finally any code correcting t arbitrary errors has distance at least2t+1. Puncturing2t positions must be injective, giving M≤b^{n−2t}; sinceM>b^4, necessarily n≥5+2t. This proves the requested length lower bounds without a linear-code assumption.

In its first nine words instead corrupt positions1 and7 by offsets54321 and98765 modulo b.","calculation":"The exact subset decoder returns the original state in both cases. The verification report retains all original and corrupted words. A word can be altered in many bits and still counts as one corruption in this model.","conclusion":"The finite decoder tests instantiate a globally proved distance theorem, and the puncturing bound proves that shorter full-population codes cannot have the same correction guarantee."}
limits: This is a coding theorem for the stated deterministic raw trajectories. It does not assert cryptographic unpredictability, statistical randomness or a correction guarantee when output positions are hidden by rejection sampling.
